AbstractText.Label: STUDY OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To describe opioid distribution and patient use after gynecologic procedures.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Survey study (Canadian Task Force classification III).

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: An urban academic tertiary care hospital.

AbstractText.Label: SUBJECTS
AbstractText.content: Ninety-six gynecologists in the Boston area, and 147 patients who underwent a benign hysterectomy between January 2015 and April 2016.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTIONS
AbstractText.content: Survey study of physicians and patients composed of 2 parts: (1) a physician survey on opioid prescribing practices after gynecologic procedures and (2) a patient survey on opioid consumption after hysterectomy. Physicians were contacted via e-mail to participate in an online survey. Eligible patients were contacted via telephone and asked to participate in a telephone survey.

AbstractText.Label: MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Fifty-one physicians responded to an online survey and prescribed a mean of 27.1 tablets (range, 5-30) of oxycodone (5 mg) or hydromorphone (2 mg) after abdominal hysterectomy (AH), a mean of 22.6 tablets (range, 5-30) after laparoscopic hysterectomy (LH), and a mean of 16.8 tablets (range 5-30) after vaginal hysterectomy (VH). Physicians prescribed more opioids for AH compared with LH, with a mean difference of 4.5 tablets (standard deviation, 4.7; p < .01), and AH compared with VH, with a mean difference of 6.8 tablets (standard deviation, 5.8; p < .01), which were both statistically significant. In addition, 40.0% of physicians prescribe opioids after a hysteroscopy and 19.2% after a dilation and curettage. Fifty-six patients participated in the telephone survey: 64.6% of patients used less than half of the opioids prescribed and 16.1% used none. For AH, patients reported being prescribed a mean of 25.7 tablets and using a mean of 8.7 tablets (range, 0-60; 33.9% used). For LH or VH, patients reported being prescribed a mean of 24.2 tablets and using a mean of 10.0 tablets (range, 0-30; 41.4% used). Opioid consumption was not significantly different for AH compared with LH or VH (p = .613 for AH to LH, p = .279 for AH to VH).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: With respect to the physician survey, we conclude there is a wide range of opioid prescription practices and patient opioid consumption after gynecologic surgery. The patient survey revealed that physicians prescribe fewer opioid tablets after a minimally invasive approach to hysterectomy versus open hysterectomy. However, most patients use less than half of prescribed opioids, and a fraction did not use any opioids at all.
